title: Wisdom as practice
hook: the sixth: seeing things as they are, in every act

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth perfection: meditation, a steady mind built one sitting at a time.

A coin, a bowl of rice, an hour of your time handed to someone who needs it. That's giving, the first perfection. But a gift can be given to show off. A precept can be kept with a sneer at the people who don't keep it. Patience can be gritted teeth, effort can be pride, and even a quiet mind can be one more thing to own. Something has to turn each of these into the real thing. In the Mahayana list, that something comes last, as the sixth, and the other five lean on it. You met the short sutra named for it early on the path. Today, wisdom.
screen: `A GIFT CAN BE GIVEN TO SHOW OFF.` → `WHAT TURNS IT INTO THE REAL THING?` → `THE SIXTH.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is prajna, in Pali panna: wisdom, understanding, the mind that sees. In the old suttas, the phrase that goes with it is seeing things as they really are. And what is that? The Dhammapada puts it in three short verses: all conditioned things pass away; all conditioned things are suffering, unable to fully satisfy; all things are without a self. When a person sees this with wisdom, the verses say, they grow weary of suffering, and that is the path to purity. So wisdom here isn't knowing lots of facts. It's seeing, right in the middle of a moment, that this too is changing, this too can't hold me up forever, and this too is not a solid me. Now the Mahayana turn. A whole family of sutras is named for this perfection: prajnaparamita, the perfection of wisdom. The short Heart Sutra belongs to it. Some of these texts compare the first five perfections to people who cannot see, and wisdom to the guide who leads them to the city. Without it, giving is just handing things over. With it, the giver sees no solid giver, no solid gift, no solid receiver to cling to, and gives freely anyway. So wisdom isn't a sixth task added at the end of the list. It's the light the other five are done by: giving, keeping precepts, patience, effort and sitting, each one done with the eyes open.
screen: `PRAJNA: THE MIND THAT SEES.` · `CHANGING, UNSATISFYING, NOT SELF.` · `THE GUIDE WHO LEADS THE BLIND.` · then, large: `WISDOM IN EVERY ACT.`

segments.voice: Choose something small in front of you, a cup, your hand, the light on a wall, and look at it for a few breaths, as it is. Notice that it's changing, even slowly, and can't stay exactly like this; then turn the same gentle look on a feeling you have right now, restlessness or ease, which is changing too. No need to think hard; just see it, and let the seeing be enough.
Wisdom as practice. Prajna, the sixth perfection: seeing things as they are, the light every other perfection is done by. Today's word.
Your line: the sixth perfection. This is changing: three words that fit in the middle of washing up or waiting in line. Six perfections, all here.

howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists count wisdom (prajna) as the sixth perfection and chant texts like the Heart Sutra from the perfection of wisdom sutras; in Theravada, wisdom (panna) is developed by seeing impermanence, unsatisfactoriness and not-self in daily experience.

options: doing them with wisdom, seeing things as they are.

original.note: Sanskrit prajna (Pali panna): wisdom, understanding; the sixth perfection, and the root of prajnaparamita, the perfection of wisdom.

trapdoor: what you thought: wisdom is being clever or well read.
what it means: prajna, seeing things as they are, and doing every good act with that seeing.
what a scholar hears: the Dhammapada's verses on impermanence, suffering and not-self, and the perfection of wisdom sutras where wisdom guides the other perfections.

chat.says: If someone's already generous and patient, why does wisdom matter so much?
options: Wisdom is the light the others are done by; without it, a gift can just be showing off.
It doesn't much. Generosity and patience are complete on their own, seeing or not.
Wisdom means knowing the sutras well, so it only really matters for scholars.
chat.meaning: Some perfection of wisdom texts call wisdom the guide who leads the other five; with it, giving and patience are done with the eyes open.

prajna.meaning: wisdom, the mind that sees things as they are

prajnaparamita.meaning: the perfection of wisdom; also a family of sutras

Heart Sutra.meaning: a short sutra in the perfection of wisdom family

Dhammapada.meaning: a collection of short verses of the Buddha's teaching

sources.ref: Astasahasrika Prajnaparamita (perfection of wisdom in 8,000 lines), the simile of the blind and the guide

notes: Dhammapada 277–279 paraphrased (Max Muller 1881 exists but wording not quoted for safety); 'three short verses' is the cited verse range. Confirm paraphrase, especially 'grow weary of suffering' and 'path to purity'.
The simile of the first five perfections as blind people and wisdom as the guide is attributed to the Astasahasrika (chapter 7 in some editions); framed as 'some of these texts'. Confirm the source.
'Seeing things as they really are' (yathabhuta) given as the phrase that goes with wisdom in the suttas; confirm.
The threefold emptiness of giver, gift and receiver is a standard Mahayana teaching on dana with prajna; confirm framing.
Pronunciation of prajna as PRUJ-nyah; regional pronunciations vary. Confirm.
